questions.question: Define biodiversity and explain its three levels with one example each.
questions.answer: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth — all the living things that share an area or the planet. Three levels: (i) SPECIES diversity — different KINDS of living things (mango tree vs neem tree). (ii) GENETIC diversity — different VARIETIES within one species (basmati vs sona masoori rice). (iii) ECOSYSTEM diversity — different KINDS OF PLACES (forest, river, desert, coral reef).

questions.question: List the SIX things a good biodiversity-register entry should include.
questions.answer: (i) Place — exact location. (ii) Habitat — what the place is like. (iii) Living thing — local + scientific name if known. (iv) Description — colour, size, behaviour. (v) Date and time. (vi) Use or relationship + notes / source. (Honest uncertainty is fine — 'possibly X'.)

questions.question: List FOUR habitats around a typical school and one living thing in each.
questions.answer: (i) Trees and bushes — sparrows / squirrels / lichens. (ii) Ground — ants / beetles / spiders / fallen leaves. (iii) Soil — earthworms / soil microbes. (iv) Walls and stones — gecko lizard / spider / lichen. (v) Water (if there is a pond) — tadpoles / algae / water-striders. (vi) Air — butterflies / bees. Any four.

questions.question: List FOUR principles of GOOD field observation.
questions.answer: (i) Look quietly for at least 2–3 minutes; let the living thing forget you are there. (ii) Sketch and describe — note colour, size, behaviour. (iii) Record place, time and weather. (iv) Be HONEST about uncertainty — 'possibly X' is fine. (v) Never catch, hurt or take living things. Any four.

questions.question: Apart from your own observations, name THREE useful sources of information for a register and one strength of each.
questions.answer: (i) Local people (farmers, elders, gardeners) — know local names, uses and history of the area. (ii) Field guides — illustrated, specific to your region, often in your language. (iii) School library / encyclopaedias / NCERT science books — give classification and scientific facts. (iv) Reliable websites (iNaturalist, India Biodiversity Portal) — quick identification + cross-check. Any three.

questions.question: Why is keeping a biodiversity register a small but real act of CONSERVATION?
questions.answer: Because the register makes us PAY ATTENTION to the living things around us. We notice changes — fewer butterflies than last year, a tree about to be cut. With clear records, we can ARGUE to protect the place: ask the school not to cut a particular tree, keep a corner unmanaged for wild plants, or get a pond cleaned. Knowledge informs action: 'what is measured gets cared for.'

questions.question: Plan how you and your group will run a 4-week BIODIVERSITY REGISTER project at your school. Include: (i) which habitats you will cover, (ii) when you will visit, (iii) what tools you will carry, (iv) what each register entry will contain, (v) how you will share findings.
questions.answer: (i) HABITATS — split the campus into six zones: trees and bushes, ground/leaf-litter, walls and stones, soil under trees, the pond / water tank if any, and the air (insects). Each pair takes one zone. (ii) WHEN — visit 3 times a week for 4 weeks; vary the time-of-day: early morning for birds, noon for insects, after rain for snails and frogs. (iii) TOOLS — small notebook, pencil, magnifying glass, measuring tape, simple field guide, phone for photos (with permission). (iv) ENTRY — each entry has place, habitat, living-thing name (local + scientific if known), date, time, weather, sketch, colour/size/behaviour, source of identification, honest 'possibly X' if not sure. (v) SHARING — at week 4 we make a poster for the corridor and a 5-slide presentation for the class. Pick three favourite living things and tell a one-minute story for each. Raise three open questions for the school to think about.

questions.question: Suppose your school is planning to cut down an old peepal tree in the playground because it 'casts too much shade'. Use ideas from this chapter to argue, with evidence, that the tree should be kept.
questions.answer: I would use the school biodiversity register as evidence. Over the past 4 weeks our register shows the peepal tree alone hosts at least 12 different living things — sparrows, mynas, butterflies, ants, lichens, even a small gecko. The tree is also a pollinator stop for bees. If we cut it, we lose all those species at once and the small ecosystem services they give: bees pollinate our kitchen-garden brinjals, birds eat insects that would otherwise eat crops, the tree itself cools the playground in summer. Across India, frog and butterfly populations have shrunk because habitats like this are cleared. Instead of cutting the tree, I would propose: (a) trim the lower branches to reduce shade where shade is unwanted, (b) keep the tree as a 'biodiversity corner' for next year's school projects, (c) plant a smaller tree nearby that grows faster but does not host as much life. Conservation does not always mean 'never change' — it means changing thoughtfully, after looking at the evidence we have collected.
questions.explanation: Use register evidence + ecosystem services + alternative.
